Loaded wants_to_leave_early. Its instructions:

# Wants to leave early

Rests on 83.595 (the landlord's choices), 83.43 (a fee, a deposit), 83.49 (the 7-day notice), 83.682 and 83.64 (servicemembers), 83.63 (damage), 83.512 (flooding), 83.46, 83.57, and 83.575 (no set end date), 83.56 and 83.505 (delivering notices), 83.47 (void clauses), 83.48 (attorney fees), and 83.59 and 83.67 (abandonment, belongings). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets both readings, and you choose neither.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- The landlord has failed to make a repair or keep a lease promise, and that is part of why they want out: load repair_not_made too. Its option 1 is a way to end the lease; do not repeat it here.
- The landlord sent a notice saying the tenant broke the lease: load notice_received_violation too. Its "Moving out" part says what is not settled about rent after a landlord ends the lease.
- The tenant has already moved out and asks about the deposit: load deposit_not_returned.
- The lease has no set end date (month to month, or no term stated (83.46(2))): leaving is not early. Written notice ends it, delivered a way 83.56(4) names, by the rent period (83.57(1) to (4)); for month to month "by giving not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)). The last day for that: count_days(period_end, -30), with period_end the last day of the month they plan to end on. A tenant who stayed on with the landlord's permission after a set term ended, and leaves without that notice: "the tenant is liable to the landlord for an additional 1 month’s rent." (83.575(3)). For a tenancy that was month to month from the start, that is not settled. One: (3) names the month-to-month notice, so it applies. The other: the section is about a tenancy "with specific duration" (83.575), so it does not. The 7 days' notice below also applies to them. The options below do not.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the end date; ending early and what is owed for it; notice before leaving; subletting or a replacement; and who else signed. Quote each clause and cite it.

- A set charge for leaving early, whatever the lease calls it (a fee, a re-rental charge, losing the deposit): "“Early termination fee” means any charge, fee, or forfeiture that is provided for in a written rental agreement and is assessed to a tenant when a tenant elects to terminate the rental agreement, as provided in the agreement, and vacates a dwelling unit before the end of the rental agreement." (83.43(6)). If it is not that, it is liquidated damages, which the stored text does not define. Either way the name does not save it: 83.595(4) covers both, and it counts only if it meets option 5's conditions. The definition leaves out rent and charges through the end of the month the landlord retakes the home, charges for damage, and a deal to settle or buy out the lease (83.43(6)).
- Any other clause setting what happens on leaving early, such as all the remaining rent falling due at once: 83.595 lists no such choice. Whether the clause stands is not settled. One: it is void to the extent it "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)), or it is a charge that needs option 5's conditions, since the definition leaves out rent only through that month. The other: 83.595 says what the landlord may do after a tenant leaves and does not bar a term both sides agreed to.
- A clause on subletting or a replacement tenant: say what it says. The stored text does not speak to subletting; anything past the lease's words is outside this tool.
- Someone else signed and stays: the stored text does not say what happens when one of several tenants leaves. Say what the lease says about each signer's share of the rent.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- planned_move_out: the date they plan to move out. lease_end_date: the date the lease ends.
- reason: why they want to leave, in their words.
- leaving_notice_given: the date they gave the landlord a written notice that they are leaving, how it went, and whether it gave an address.
- early_addendum: only if the lease you hold does not show it, whether they signed a separate paper about a fee for leaving early, which box is marked, and the amount.
- Only if the reason points to one: orders (what the military orders say, and how far away), servicemember_notice_received (the date the landlord received the written notice), damage_date and what was damaged (and who or what caused it), flood_loss_date.

## How to answer

Give only the options the facts point to, and name the others in one line (military orders, damage to the home, flooding, a landlord who failed a duty), so the tenant can say if one fits. When the facts point to none of those, say that part II names no right to end a lease with a set end date just because the tenant wants to move. The tenant can move out, but moving out or giving notice does not by itself end the lease or stop the rent. What they owe then depends on options 4 to 6.

## Option 1: military orders

All of these must be met.

1. **A servicemember.** The term has "the same meaning as provided in s. 250.01" (83.43(15)), which is not stored; the tenant can say whether they are one.
2. **One of the listed grounds** (83.682(1)(a) to (f)). Ask what the orders say:
   - "required, pursuant to a permanent change of station orders, to move 35 miles or more from the location of the rental premises" (83.682(1)(a));
   - "prematurely or involuntarily discharged or released from active duty or state active duty" (83.682(1)(b));
   - released from active duty after leasing while on active duty, with the home 35 miles or more from the home of record (83.682(1)(c));
   - "After entering into a rental agreement" (83.682(1)(d)), orders into government quarters, or becoming eligible for them and choosing to move there (83.682(1)(d));
   - "temporary duty orders, temporary change of station orders, or state active duty orders to an area 35 miles or more from the location of the rental premises, provided such orders are for a period exceeding 60 days" (83.682(1)(e));
   - a change of orders to 35 miles or more away, before moving in (83.682(1)(f)).
   Orders or a move that fit none of these: not met. Say so in one sentence and go on to the other options.
3. **A written notice with proof.** "The notice to the landlord must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer." (83.682(2)).
4. **The date.** The notice takes effect "on the date stated in the notice which is at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice" (83.682(1)). The earliest date: count_days(servicemember_notice_received, 30). Before the landlord has it, the last day it must arrive to end the lease on the planned date: count_days(planned_move_out, -30).

What it gives: "the tenant is liable for the rent due under the rental agreement prorated to the effective date of the termination" (83.682(4)), and "The tenant is not liable for any other rent or damages due to the early termination of the tenancy as provided for in this section." (83.682(4)). Terminating 14 or more days before moving in: "no damages or penalties of any kind will be assessable." (83.682(4)). "The provisions of this section may not be waived or modified by the agreement of the parties under any circumstances." (83.682(5)). The landlord may not retaliate for it (83.64(1)(d)). Do not work out the prorated amount.

If the tenant also signed an addendum for a fee or liquidated damages, it is not owed; say so plainly. Ending the lease this way is a right, not a breach, and 83.595 opens "If the tenant breaches the rental agreement" (83.595). A fee is assessed when a tenant terminates "as provided in the agreement" (83.43(6)), and this termination is under the statute. Liquidated damages are damages, which (4) rules out. And no agreement can change this section (83.682(5)).

If the servicemember died on active duty, an adult in the immediate family may end the lease the same way, with the death certificate (83.682(3)).

## Option 2: the home was damaged

"If the premises are damaged or destroyed other than by the wrongful or negligent acts of the tenant so that the enjoyment of the premises is substantially impaired" (83.63), then:

- "The tenant may terminate the rental agreement and immediately vacate the premises." (83.63(1)). The section names no notice and no waiting period.
- Or: "The tenant may vacate the part of the premises rendered unusable by the casualty, in which case the tenant’s liability for rent shall be reduced by the fair rental value of that part of the premises damaged or destroyed." (83.63(1)).

Settle what was damaged, how much of the home it took out of use, and who caused it. The stored text does not define "substantially impaired" (83.63): set the tenant's facts beside the words and state no test of your own. Whether a slow problem, like a leak or mold that builds up, is this kind of damage is not settled. Load repair_not_made for the other route. One: "damaged or destroyed" (83.63) reaches any damage that does this, and the text never says it must be sudden. The other: the word "casualty" (83.63(1)) may suggest a sudden event. If the lease ends this way, "the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3)." (83.63(1)), the deposit rules. The tenant must get the chance to collect belongings when it is safe, or notice of a date within a reasonable time (83.63(2)).

## Option 3: flooding, with no flood disclosure

All of these must be met.

1. **A lease of a year or longer, with no disclosure.** "A landlord must complete and provide a flood disclosure to a prospective tenant of residential real property at or before the execution of a rental agreement for a term of 1 year or longer." (83.512(1)). "The flood disclosure must be in a separate document." (83.512(1)). Read the lease's papers, and ask whether they got one. A paper that is blank or false: not settled whether that is a violation, since the rule says "complete and provide" (83.512(1)). The stored text does not say from what date the section applies (its history note cites ch. 2025-166); say so, and that this is outside the tool.
2. **A substantial loss from flooding.** "the total cost of repairs to or replacement of the personal property is 50 percent or more of the personal property’s market value on the date the flooding occurred." (83.512(2)). The tenant can give the amounts. The disclosure's form defines flooding as overflowing water, runoff, and standing rainwater (83.512(1)); not settled whether that limits (2), so that a burst pipe is left out.
3. **Notice and leaving in time.** "by giving a written notice of termination and surrendering possession of the premises to the landlord no later than 30 days after the date of the damage or loss." (83.512(2)). The last day: count_days(flood_loss_date, 30).

What it gives: the lease ends when they give up the home (83.512(2)); the landlord refunds "all rent or other amounts paid in advance under the rental agreement for any period after the effective date of the termination of the rental agreement." (83.512(3)). Rent unpaid from before that date is still owed (83.512(4)).

## Option 4: a deal with the landlord

The landlord may agree to let them go. Charges tied to a "rental agreement settlement, release, buyout, or accord and satisfaction agreement" (83.43(6)) are not an early termination fee, so option 5's limits do not apply to the price. Say what the lease requires for a change (a writing, signed, if it says so), and that the deal should say in writing what is owed and that nothing more is. A "buyout" clause already in the lease from the start: not settled whether it is such a deal or a fee under option 5.

## Option 5: pay the fee the tenant agreed to

All of these must be met.

1. **A separate signed addendum, from when the lease was made.** "This remedy is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee." (83.595(4)). "The tenant must indicate acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement" (83.595(4)).
   - A separate signed paper with "I agree" marked, or words that agree to the amount: met.
   - The charge is only in the body of the lease, or "I do not agree" is marked, or no choice is marked: not met. Say plainly the fee cannot be charged this way, whatever the lease says, and go to option 6.
2. **The amount.** "if the amount does not exceed 2 months’ rent" (83.595(4)). Set it beside two months of the lease's rent. If it is more: not met, and the fee falls away; nothing in 83.595(4) cuts an amount down to the limit. Say so plainly, and go to option 6.
3. **For a fee, the notice.** "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination." (83.595(4)). Read the lease's notice period. If it is more than 60 days: not met for a fee. The words apply only "in the case of an early termination fee" (83.595(4)). If the paper names both a fee and liquidated damages and asks more than 60 days, whether this limit applies is not settled.

What it costs: the amount, and "the rent and other charges accrued through the end of the month in which the landlord retakes possession of the dwelling unit and charges for damages to the dwelling unit." (83.595(4)(a)).

What the landlord gives up: the statute's form says "the landlord waives the right to seek additional rent beyond the month in which the landlord retakes possession." (83.595(4)). If the tenant's addendum says so, say plainly that the landlord gave that up. If it leaves those words out, it is not settled whether it is still the addendum the statute asks for. One: the form need only be followed "substantially" (83.595(4)), so the fee stands. The other: those words are what the tenant gets for the fee, so without them there is no fee under option 5, and option 6 applies.

The tenant's notice under the lease: if the lease gives a number of days, the last day is count_days(planned_move_out, -N), with N that number. If it is in months, give the lease's words; the tool counts days only. This subsection does not reach a failure to give the end-of-lease notice in 83.575 (83.595(4)(b)).

## Option 6: move out, and the landlord chooses

"If the tenant breaches the rental agreement for the dwelling unit and the landlord has obtained a writ of possession, or the tenant has surrendered possession of the dwelling unit to the landlord, or the tenant has abandoned the dwelling unit, the landlord may:" (83.595). The choice is the landlord's. Set each beside the tenant's rent and lease end date, in words:

- End it: "Treat the rental agreement as terminated and retake possession for his or her own account, thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant" (83.595(1)).
- Re-rent it for the tenant: "holding the tenant liable for the difference between the rent stipulated to be paid under the rental agreement and what the landlord is able to recover from a reletting." (83.595(2)). The landlord "has a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (83.595(2)), which means at least the same efforts as for the first rental or for its similar units, with no need to prefer this home over its other vacant ones (83.595(2)). Rent received is deducted.
- Wait: "Stand by and do nothing, holding the lessee liable for the rent as it comes due" (83.595(3)).
- The fee, only if option 5's conditions are met. Without them the landlord has the first three; say so.

Say the rent for the rest of the lease, through the end date.

Also: a suit cuts both ways, since the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). The deposit may go toward the loss, since security deposits cover "monetary damage to the landlord caused by the tenant’s breach of lease prior to the expiration thereof." (83.43(14)), but only by the steps in 83.49(3); a lease clause that simply takes it is an early termination fee (above). After the move, deposit_not_returned covers those steps. Court steps and amounts are outside this tool.

A tenant who just stops coming may be treated as having abandoned the home: "In the absence of actual knowledge of abandonment, it shall be presumed that the tenant has abandoned the dwelling unit if he or she is absent from the premises for a period of time equal to one-half the time for periodic rental payments." (83.59(3)(c)), unless the rent is current or they told the landlord in writing of an intended absence (83.59(3)(c)). The landlord may remove what they leave behind after "surrender, abandonment" (83.67(5)); read the lease for a clause on it. A landlord need not pay deposit interest to a tenant who wrongfully ended the tenancy early (83.49(9)).

## Whichever way they leave: the 7 days' notice

Any tenant moving out before the end date, and any tenant with no set end date. It keeps the landlord's duty to send a notice about the deposit. Say in the same breath that it does not end the lease or stop the rent.

- Options 1 and 3 have their own written notice. The stored text does not say whether this one applies too; one written notice by hand or certified mail, with the address, in time for both, meets both.
- Option 2 says "immediately vacate" (83.63(1)) and that the landlord shall follow 83.49(3). Whether a tenant leaving at once still needs these 7 days is not settled. One: the rule names "any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term" (83.49(5)). The other: 83.63 sets its own terms.
- The rule: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)), the tenant "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
- The last day: count_days(planned_move_out, -7), counted back from the move. The stored text does not say whether a certified letter counts from mailing or arrival; handing it over, or mailing it early, meets both.
- Handed over or certified mail, with an address: met. E-mail only under the signed addendum in 83.505(1). A portal message, a text, or regular mail is not one of the ways named.
- The lease has a clause on notice before leaving: read it. A different rule for leaving governs. Whether a clause on some other notice, like the notice before paying a fee, is one that "otherwise provided" (83.49(5)) is not settled; one notice in time for both, by hand or certified mail, with the address, meets both.
- If it is missed: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying a tenant may end a lease with a set end date just by giving notice when no way out fits, or that the 7 days' notice ends the lease or stops the rent.
- Stating one total owed, saying which choice the landlord will make, or counting the months left or the rent left.
- Saying the landlord must re-rent the home in every case. The duty is in 83.595(2) only.
- Applying a fee, a charge, or a loss of the deposit without the separate signed addendum and the other conditions, or treating what the lease calls a charge as deciding what it is.
- Leaving out what is still owed with a fee (83.595(4)(a)), or the prorated rent for a servicemember (83.682(4)).
- Missing a way out the facts point to.
- Counting the 7 days forward from the notice instead of back from the move.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

Whether a local building or housing code also covers this is outside what I can check. The city or county code office can tell you.

### Did your portal requests count as the notice to end the lease?
No. To end the lease, the statute requires the landlord to fail to fix a problem "within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof" (§ 83.56(1)).
- Your requests asked for a repair. You told me neither one mentions ending the lease.
- The statute says notices are delivered "by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (§ 83.56(4)). A portal message is not on that list.
- Your lease says the same. Notices to the landlord must be "delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail" (Lease § 7).
- Your lease also says you and the landlord have not agreed to e-mail notices (Lease § 8).

So the notice should name the leak, say you will end the lease because of it, and go by hand or certified mail to the Suite A address. The 7 days run from the day it reaches the landlord, not the day you send it.

### Is the leak "material," and did paying April rent cost you the right?
Neither point is settled, so I can't say how a court would rule.
- **Material.** One reading is that any failure to keep up the roof is material. The other is that it depends on how serious the leak is, how long it has gone on, and how it affects your living there. A leak since March 20 that drips whenever it rains, with no response to two requests, supports the second reading. The statute doesn't define the word.
- **Paying rent.** A tenant who "pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" gives up the right to end the lease "for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (§ 83.56(5)(a)). One reading is that a leak that is still unfixed is a "continuing" failure, so paying rent gave up nothing. The other is that paying April rent gave up the right over this failure, and only a new failure would restart it.
- This is why the date of any further rent payment matters. I can't tell you whether paying May rent on May 1 would change things. It could add to the risk under the second reading.

### If I move out May 15 without a valid notice, what happens?
Part II names no right to end a lease with a set end date just because you want to move. The lease runs to July 31, 2026 (Lease § 3). If you leave and the repair route fails, the landlord chooses one of these (§ 83.595):
- End the lease and retake the apartment, which ends your liability.
- Re-rent the apartment for you. You would owe the gap between your rent and what the new tenant pays. The landlord must make a good-faith effort to re-rent (§ 83.595(2)).
- Wait and hold you to the rent as it comes due (§ 83.595(3)).

Your lease has no early-termination fee or addendum, so the landlord can't charge one.

### Does moving out require a separate notice?
Yes, apart from the repair notice. Before leaving early you must "give at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (§ 83.49(5)). For a May 15 move, the last day for that is May 8, 2026. Your lease also asks for a written forwarding address (Lease § 6).

This notice does not end the lease or stop the rent. It only preserves the landlord's duty to send you a notice about your security deposit. One letter can do both jobs if it is delivered in time.

### Are there other options?
- **Damage to the home.** If the home is damaged so that "the enjoyment of the premises is substantially impaired" and you didn't cause it, you may end the lease and vacate (§ 83.63(1)). It is not settled whether a slow leak counts. One reading is that "damaged" covers any damage of that kind. The other is that the word "casualty" points to a sudden event.
- **Code complaint.** A complaint to the code office can bring an inspection. It is also protected from retaliation by the landlord (§ 83.64(1)).

Loaded repair_not_made. Its instructions:

# Repair not made

Rests on 83.51 (repairs), 83.56 (ending the lease, notices, rent paid), 83.60 (holding back rent), 83.55 (damages), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.47 (void lease clauses), 83.48 (attorney fees), 83.59 (actions for possession), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- "The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant." (83.51(1)).
- If the landlord has filed an eviction case, see "If the landlord sues" under option 2. Court steps beyond what this skill says are outside this tool.
- If the tenant ended the lease and moved out, load deposit_not_returned for the deposit.

## Whose job the repair is

Ask what broke, in plain words. Never ask whether it is "structural", a "code" matter, or "material".

1. **What 83.51(1) requires.** The landlord must "Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (83.51(1)(a)), or, where there are none, "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (83.51(1)(b)). Screens: in reasonable condition when the tenancy starts, then damage repaired once a year when needed (83.51(1)).
   - The structure or the plumbing: an 83.51(1) duty.
   - Whether a code covers the problem: outside the tool, since the codes are not stored; the city or county code office can say and inspect.
   - "The landlord's obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex." (83.51(1)). For a house or duplex, read the lease's repair clause and ask whether they signed anything else about repairs; say what it says. For any other home, the statute gives no such change.
2. **What 83.51(2)(a) adds,** for a home other than a single-family home or duplex, "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)): "The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs." (83.51(2)(a)); locks and keys; clean and safe common areas; garbage removal; and "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water." (83.51(2)(a)).
   - These are not a defense to eviction: "Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59" (83.51(2)(c)). 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) speak only of 83.51(1), so an item only (2) names reaches option 1 only if a code or the lease also covers it, and option 2 only if a code does.
   - Pest treatment: "If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent." (83.51(2)(a)). The landlord gives 7 days' written notice when the tenant must leave for it, and the tenant need leave for at most 4 days (83.51(2)(a)).
   - Running water and hot water: not settled which list holds them. The plumbing is in 83.51(1)(b), and (2)(a) names them too. "If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord's duty is determined by subsection (1)." (83.51(3)). Give both readings and choose neither. One: the failure is in the plumbing, so it is an 83.51(1) duty and options 1 and 2 reach it. The other: (2)(a) names it, so it is a (2) duty, which 83.51(2)(c) keeps out of a defense to eviction. Heat is named only in (2)(a), so it is a (2) duty unless a code or the lease covers it.
3. **What the lease adds.** Anything the lease says comes with the home, or that the landlord will keep up, counts, whatever it is and whether or not this skill names it. Read the whole lease for the broken or closed item: whether the lease promises it, who repairs it, any clause on closing it, and any fee for it. Quote the clause and cite its section.
   - The lease promises the item, or says the landlord repairs it: a lease duty. Options 1, 3, and 4 can reach it. Option 2 never does, since it rests on 83.51(1) alone. Say so plainly when the tenant asks about holding back rent.
   - An item neither of 83.51's lists names is the landlord's job only if the lease says so or a local code requires it (outside the tool). Never say 83.51 requires it. Air conditioning is a common one.
   - Two examples of the handling, not a list. A dishwasher the lease provides breaks: 83.51 does not name it, so it is a lease promise; ending the lease may reach it (material is not settled), holding back rent does not, damages may. A pool the lease lets the landlord close for cleaning stays closed a month: read that clause first; whether it limits the promise is the open question below.
   - The lease puts a repair on the tenant, or says an item may be closed or is offered only as a courtesy: say what it says. For a house or duplex, a writing may change the 83.51(1) duty (above). For an item only 83.51(2)(a) names, a writing may change it in any home, since the paragraph applies "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)). Otherwise, a clause is void "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) does either of two things: "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)) or limits a party's liability under law (83.47(1)(b)). Whether a clause that limits an amenity itself (its hours, its closures) is such a clause is not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it only says what the lease promises, so it stands, and the promise is what it describes. The other: it takes away a right part II gives (ending the lease under 83.56(1), damages under 83.55), so it is void to that extent.
4. **Who caused it.** "The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant's family, or other person on the premises with the tenant's consent." (83.51(4)).
   - Nothing anyone did (age, wear, weather), the landlord or its workers, or someone the tenant did not let in: the landlord's, as far as 83.51(4) goes.
   - The tenant, a family member, or a guest they let in: not the landlord's under 83.51. Say so in one sentence, and say what the lease says about who pays.
   - A roommate: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither, and ask how the roommate came to live there. One: a roommate sharing the home is there with the tenant's consent, so 83.51(4) applies. The other: a roommate the landlord placed under a lease of their own is there by the landlord's leave, so 83.51(4) does not reach what they caused.
   - The tenant does not know: a work order, a repair person's note, or the landlord's messages may show it.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- problem: what broke, in the tenant's words, and which part of the home.
- problem_noticed_date: when they first noticed it.
- home_type: a single-family house, a duplex, or a unit in a larger building.
- cause: who or what caused it, as far as they know.
- repair_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will end the lease over the problem reached the landlord. Also note how it went (handed over, mailed, e-mail, portal, text) and what it says about ending the lease.
- withhold_notice_delivered: the date a written notice saying they will not pay rent over the problem reached the landlord, and who received it.
- rent_paid_since: whether they paid rent after they knew of the problem.
- eviction_filed: whether the landlord has filed an eviction case.
- code_complaint_date: the date they complained to a code office, if they did.

A notice counts from the day it reached the landlord, not the day it was sent. If the tenant gives only the day it was sent, ask when it arrived (the day it was handed over, or a mail receipt). The exception is e-mail under 83.505: "A notice sent electronically pursuant to this section is deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)).

## Option 1: end the lease

The rule: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(1)).

All four conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, not settled, or outside the tool.

1. **A duty the landlord failed.** An 83.51(1) duty, or a material provision of the lease (see "Whose job the repair is"). Whether the failure is "material" (83.56(1)) is not settled: the stored text does not define the word. Give both readings and choose neither, setting the tenant's facts beside the word. One: any failure of a duty 83.51(1) lists, or of a lease promise, is material. The other: it turns on how serious the problem is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, that names the problem and says they will end the lease.** "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (83.56(4)). A lease cannot waive these notice rules (83.56(4)).
   - Handed to the landlord or the office, or mailed: delivered.
   - E-mail: only if all of 83.505(1)'s conditions are met, "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices and have each provided a valid e-mail address for such purpose, and the addendum conspicuously advises the parties that such election is voluntary and that they may revoke such agreement or update their e-mail addresses at any time." (83.505(1)). Read the lease for such an addendum and say what it shows.
   - A portal message or a text: not one of the ways 83.56(4) names; sending it again by hand or by mail meets the rule.
   - The words: set the tenant's notice beside the statute's. A message that asks for a repair but does not say they will end the lease is not this notice. Say so in one sentence.
3. **Seven days passed without the repair.** Call count_days(repair_notice_delivered, 7). If the date has not passed, the landlord still has time; give the date.
4. **Not given up by paying rent.** If "the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).
   - No rent paid since they knew of the problem: met.
   - Rent paid while the problem goes on: not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a problem still not fixed is a "continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), so paying rent gives up nothing. The other: paying rent with knowledge gives up ending the lease over that failure, and only a new failure starts over.

If all four are met, say plainly that the tenant may end the lease (83.56(1)).

Option 2's notice is not one of these four conditions. A tenant who asks to move out and stop paying rent is asking about this option, not option 2. If the landlord sues for unpaid rent (83.60(1)(a) names "an action by the landlord under s. 83.55 seeking to recover unpaid rent"), the tenant "may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable, that he or she may have" (83.60(1)(a)); only the defense of "a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)" needs option 2's notice (83.60(1)(b)).

## Option 2: hold back rent, and raise the problem if sued

Say first, in plain words, that holding back rent risks an eviction case, and what the tenant must do if sued (below).

The rule: "The defense of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) may be raised by the tenant if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof." (83.60(1)(b)). What it gives: "A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent" (83.60(1)(b)), and the court decides how much, if any, the rent is reduced for that time (83.60(1)(b)).

All four conditions must be met.

1. **An 83.51(1) duty, and only that.** Never an item only the lease promises, whatever it is, and never an item only 83.51(2) names. For running and hot water, give the two readings above. Whether the failure is material is not settled, as in option 1.
2. **The written notice.** It names the problem and says they will not pay rent because of it. It may go to the landlord, its designated representative, a resident manager, or whoever collects the rent (83.60(1)(b)). How it must be delivered is not settled, since 83.60(1)(b) names no way. Give both readings and choose neither. One: a written notice that reaches one of those people counts however it was sent, e-mail and portal included. The other: part II's ways for notices apply (83.56(4)), so e-mail counts only under the 83.505 addendum, and a portal message or a text does not. Handing it over or mailing it meets both readings; say so.
3. **Seven days passed.** Call count_days(withhold_notice_delivered, 7).
4. **The tenant's side did not cause it** (see "Who caused it").

If the landlord sues: "the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant's defenses other than payment" (83.60(2)). Paying, or filing that motion, in time keeps the defenses. "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; say the summons states the requirement.

## Option 3: damages

"If either the landlord or the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of the rental agreement or this part, the aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." (83.55). It reaches 83.51 duties and lease promises alike, with no notice named. Rent paid with knowledge may give up the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)) too; give option 1's two readings. A suit cuts both ways: the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool.

## Option 4: a code complaint, and protection from retaliation

A code office can inspect (outside the tool; see "Whose job the repair is"). The protection: "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Its examples include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)) and a repair notice under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)).

- The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)).
- Being treated differently in the rent, the services, or the action taken is required (83.64(4)).
- It is a defense in an action for possession (83.64(2)).
- Not when the landlord shows good cause: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)). Its examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)), so for a tenant sued over rent they held back, option 2 is the defense to look at.
- Whether the landlord acted primarily to retaliate is for a court. Give the dates of the complaint and of the landlord's act as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## Option 5: when the landlord is trying but cannot fix it

When the failure of an 83.51(1) duty or a material lease provision is due to causes beyond the landlord's control, and the landlord has made and keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it, the lease "may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows:" (83.56(1)). "If the landlord's failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable." (83.56(1)(a)). "If the landlord's failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance." (83.56(1)(b)).

- Whether the cause is beyond the landlord's control, and whether it keeps making every reasonable effort: ask what the landlord has said and done about the problem. The stored text does not define "untenantable" (83.56(1)(a)); set the tenant's facts beside the word.
- "terminated or altered by the parties" (83.56(1)): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: both sides must agree to end or change the lease, and (a) and (b) set what follows. The other: (a) and (b) apply once their facts are met, so a tenant who leaves an untenantable home owes no rent for that time, and one who stays owes reduced rent.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Treating any written complaint as the notice in 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b). Each must say what the tenant will do: end the lease, or not pay rent.
- Making option 2's notice a condition of ending the lease under option 1.
- Saying the tenant may hold back rent over an item only the lease or 83.51(2) names.
- Saying 83.51 requires an item its lists do not name, such as air conditioning.
- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, counting the days between two dates, or counting a 7-day period from the day a notice was sent instead of delivered (except an e-mail under 83.505).
- Explaining holding back rent without its risk and 83.60(2), or giving a calendar date for its 5 days.
- Stating a standard for "material", "untenantable", or "good faith" that the statute does not give.
- Leaving out 83.56(5)(a) when the tenant paid rent after knowing of the problem.
- Treating damage the tenant, their family, or a guest caused as the landlord's under 83.51.

# Wants to leave early

Rests on 83.595 (the landlord's choices), 83.43 (a fee, a deposit), 83.49 (the 7-day notice), 83.682 and 83.64 (servicemembers), 83.63 (damage), 83.512 (flooding), 83.46, 83.57, and 83.575 (no set end date), 83.56 and 83.505 (delivering notices), 83.47 (void clauses), 83.48 (attorney fees), and 83.59 and 83.67 (abandonment, belongings). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets both readings, and you choose neither.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- The landlord has failed to make a repair or keep a lease promise, and that is part of why they want out: load repair_not_made too. Its option 1 is a way to end the lease; do not repeat it here.
- The landlord sent a notice saying the tenant broke the lease: load notice_received_violation too. Its "Moving out" part says what is not settled about rent after a landlord ends the lease.
- The tenant has already moved out and asks about the deposit: load deposit_not_returned.
- The lease has no set end date (month to month, or no term stated (83.46(2))): leaving is not early. Written notice ends it, delivered a way 83.56(4) names, by the rent period (83.57(1) to (4)); for month to month "by giving not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)). The last day for that: count_days(period_end, -30), with period_end the last day of the month they plan to end on. A tenant who stayed on with the landlord's permission after a set term ended, and leaves without that notice: "the tenant is liable to the landlord for an additional 1 month’s rent." (83.575(3)). For a tenancy that was month to month from the start, that is not settled. One: (3) names the month-to-month notice, so it applies. The other: the section is about a tenancy "with specific duration" (83.575), so it does not. The 7 days' notice below also applies to them. The options below do not.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the end date; ending early and what is owed for it; notice before leaving; subletting or a replacement; and who else signed. Quote each clause and cite it.

- A set charge for leaving early, whatever the lease calls it (a fee, a re-rental charge, losing the deposit): "“Early termination fee” means any charge, fee, or forfeiture that is provided for in a written rental agreement and is assessed to a tenant when a tenant elects to terminate the rental agreement, as provided in the agreement, and vacates a dwelling unit before the end of the rental agreement." (83.43(6)). If it is not that, it is liquidated damages, which the stored text does not define. Either way the name does not save it: 83.595(4) covers both, and it counts only if it meets option 5's conditions. The definition leaves out rent and charges through the end of the month the landlord retakes the home, charges for damage, and a deal to settle or buy out the lease (83.43(6)).
- Any other clause setting what happens on leaving early, such as all the remaining rent falling due at once: 83.595 lists no such choice. Whether the clause stands is not settled. One: it is void to the extent it "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part." (83.47(1)(a)), or it is a charge that needs option 5's conditions, since the definition leaves out rent only through that month. The other: 83.595 says what the landlord may do after a tenant leaves and does not bar a term both sides agreed to.
- A clause on subletting or a replacement tenant: say what it says. The stored text does not speak to subletting; anything past the lease's words is outside this tool.
- Someone else signed and stays: the stored text does not say what happens when one of several tenants leaves. Say what the lease says about each signer's share of the rent.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- planned_move_out: the date they plan to move out. lease_end_date: the date the lease ends.
- reason: why they want to leave, in their words.
- leaving_notice_given: the date they gave the landlord a written notice that they are leaving, how it went, and whether it gave an address.
- early_addendum: only if the lease you hold does not show it, whether they signed a separate paper about a fee for leaving early, which box is marked, and the amount.
- Only if the reason points to one: orders (what the military orders say, and how far away), servicemember_notice_received (the date the landlord received the written notice), damage_date and what was damaged (and who or what caused it), flood_loss_date.

## How to answer

Give only the options the facts point to, and name the others in one line (military orders, damage to the home, flooding, a landlord who failed a duty), so the tenant can say if one fits. When the facts point to none of those, say that part II names no right to end a lease with a set end date just because the tenant wants to move. The tenant can move out, but moving out or giving notice does not by itself end the lease or stop the rent. What they owe then depends on options 4 to 6.

## Option 1: military orders

All of these must be met.

1. **A servicemember.** The term has "the same meaning as provided in s. 250.01" (83.43(15)), which is not stored; the tenant can say whether they are one.
2. **One of the listed grounds** (83.682(1)(a) to (f)). Ask what the orders say:
   - "required, pursuant to a permanent change of station orders, to move 35 miles or more from the location of the rental premises" (83.682(1)(a));
   - "prematurely or involuntarily discharged or released from active duty or state active duty" (83.682(1)(b));
   - released from active duty after leasing while on active duty, with the home 35 miles or more from the home of record (83.682(1)(c));
   - "After entering into a rental agreement" (83.682(1)(d)), orders into government quarters, or becoming eligible for them and choosing to move there (83.682(1)(d));
   - "temporary duty orders, temporary change of station orders, or state active duty orders to an area 35 miles or more from the location of the rental premises, provided such orders are for a period exceeding 60 days" (83.682(1)(e));
   - a change of orders to 35 miles or more away, before moving in (83.682(1)(f)).
   Orders or a move that fit none of these: not met. Say so in one sentence and go on to the other options.
3. **A written notice with proof.** "The notice to the landlord must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer." (83.682(2)).
4. **The date.** The notice takes effect "on the date stated in the notice which is at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice" (83.682(1)). The earliest date: count_days(servicemember_notice_received, 30). Before the landlord has it, the last day it must arrive to end the lease on the planned date: count_days(planned_move_out, -30).

What it gives: "the tenant is liable for the rent due under the rental agreement prorated to the effective date of the termination" (83.682(4)), and "The tenant is not liable for any other rent or damages due to the early termination of the tenancy as provided for in this section." (83.682(4)). Terminating 14 or more days before moving in: "no damages or penalties of any kind will be assessable." (83.682(4)). "The provisions of this section may not be waived or modified by the agreement of the parties under any circumstances." (83.682(5)). The landlord may not retaliate for it (83.64(1)(d)). Do not work out the prorated amount.

If the tenant also signed an addendum for a fee or liquidated damages, it is not owed; say so plainly. Ending the lease this way is a right, not a breach, and 83.595 opens "If the tenant breaches the rental agreement" (83.595). A fee is assessed when a tenant terminates "as provided in the agreement" (83.43(6)), and this termination is under the statute. Liquidated damages are damages, which (4) rules out. And no agreement can change this section (83.682(5)).

If the servicemember died on active duty, an adult in the immediate family may end the lease the same way, with the death certificate (83.682(3)).

## Option 2: the home was damaged

"If the premises are damaged or destroyed other than by the wrongful or negligent acts of the tenant so that the enjoyment of the premises is substantially impaired" (83.63), then:

- "The tenant may terminate the rental agreement and immediately vacate the premises." (83.63(1)). The section names no notice and no waiting period.
- Or: "The tenant may vacate the part of the premises rendered unusable by the casualty, in which case the tenant’s liability for rent shall be reduced by the fair rental value of that part of the premises damaged or destroyed." (83.63(1)).

Settle what was damaged, how much of the home it took out of use, and who caused it. The stored text does not define "substantially impaired" (83.63): set the tenant's facts beside the words and state no test of your own. Whether a slow problem, like a leak or mold that builds up, is this kind of damage is not settled. Load repair_not_made for the other route. One: "damaged or destroyed" (83.63) reaches any damage that does this, and the text never says it must be sudden. The other: the word "casualty" (83.63(1)) may suggest a sudden event. If the lease ends this way, "the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3)." (83.63(1)), the deposit rules. The tenant must get the chance to collect belongings when it is safe, or notice of a date within a reasonable time (83.63(2)).

## Option 3: flooding, with no flood disclosure

All of these must be met.

1. **A lease of a year or longer, with no disclosure.** "A landlord must complete and provide a flood disclosure to a prospective tenant of residential real property at or before the execution of a rental agreement for a term of 1 year or longer." (83.512(1)). "The flood disclosure must be in a separate document." (83.512(1)). Read the lease's papers, and ask whether they got one. A paper that is blank or false: not settled whether that is a violation, since the rule says "complete and provide" (83.512(1)). The stored text does not say from what date the section applies (its history note cites ch. 2025-166); say so, and that this is outside the tool.
2. **A substantial loss from flooding.** "the total cost of repairs to or replacement of the personal property is 50 percent or more of the personal property’s market value on the date the flooding occurred." (83.512(2)). The tenant can give the amounts. The disclosure's form defines flooding as overflowing water, runoff, and standing rainwater (83.512(1)); not settled whether that limits (2), so that a burst pipe is left out.
3. **Notice and leaving in time.** "by giving a written notice of termination and surrendering possession of the premises to the landlord no later than 30 days after the date of the damage or loss." (83.512(2)). The last day: count_days(flood_loss_date, 30).

What it gives: the lease ends when they give up the home (83.512(2)); the landlord refunds "all rent or other amounts paid in advance under the rental agreement for any period after the effective date of the termination of the rental agreement." (83.512(3)). Rent unpaid from before that date is still owed (83.512(4)).

## Option 4: a deal with the landlord

The landlord may agree to let them go. Charges tied to a "rental agreement settlement, release, buyout, or accord and satisfaction agreement" (83.43(6)) are not an early termination fee, so option 5's limits do not apply to the price. Say what the lease requires for a change (a writing, signed, if it says so), and that the deal should say in writing what is owed and that nothing more is. A "buyout" clause already in the lease from the start: not settled whether it is such a deal or a fee under option 5.

## Option 5: pay the fee the tenant agreed to

All of these must be met.

1. **A separate signed addendum, from when the lease was made.** "This remedy is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee." (83.595(4)). "The tenant must indicate acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement" (83.595(4)).
   - A separate signed paper with "I agree" marked, or words that agree to the amount: met.
   - The charge is only in the body of the lease, or "I do not agree" is marked, or no choice is marked: not met. Say plainly the fee cannot be charged this way, whatever the lease says, and go to option 6.
2. **The amount.** "if the amount does not exceed 2 months’ rent" (83.595(4)). Set it beside two months of the lease's rent. If it is more: not met, and the fee falls away; nothing in 83.595(4) cuts an amount down to the limit. Say so plainly, and go to option 6.
3. **For a fee, the notice.** "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination." (83.595(4)). Read the lease's notice period. If it is more than 60 days: not met for a fee. The words apply only "in the case of an early termination fee" (83.595(4)). If the paper names both a fee and liquidated damages and asks more than 60 days, whether this limit applies is not settled.

What it costs: the amount, and "the rent and other charges accrued through the end of the month in which the landlord retakes possession of the dwelling unit and charges for damages to the dwelling unit." (83.595(4)(a)).

What the landlord gives up: the statute's form says "the landlord waives the right to seek additional rent beyond the month in which the landlord retakes possession." (83.595(4)). If the tenant's addendum says so, say plainly that the landlord gave that up. If it leaves those words out, it is not settled whether it is still the addendum the statute asks for. One: the form need only be followed "substantially" (83.595(4)), so the fee stands. The other: those words are what the tenant gets for the fee, so without them there is no fee under option 5, and option 6 applies.

The tenant's notice under the lease: if the lease gives a number of days, the last day is count_days(planned_move_out, -N), with N that number. If it is in months, give the lease's words; the tool counts days only. This subsection does not reach a failure to give the end-of-lease notice in 83.575 (83.595(4)(b)).

## Option 6: move out, and the landlord chooses

"If the tenant breaches the rental agreement for the dwelling unit and the landlord has obtained a writ of possession, or the tenant has surrendered possession of the dwelling unit to the landlord, or the tenant has abandoned the dwelling unit, the landlord may:" (83.595). The choice is the landlord's. Set each beside the tenant's rent and lease end date, in words:

- End it: "Treat the rental agreement as terminated and retake possession for his or her own account, thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant" (83.595(1)).
- Re-rent it for the tenant: "holding the tenant liable for the difference between the rent stipulated to be paid under the rental agreement and what the landlord is able to recover from a reletting." (83.595(2)). The landlord "has a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (83.595(2)), which means at least the same efforts as for the first rental or for its similar units, with no need to prefer this home over its other vacant ones (83.595(2)). Rent received is deducted.
- Wait: "Stand by and do nothing, holding the lessee liable for the rent as it comes due" (83.595(3)).
- The fee, only if option 5's conditions are met. Without them the landlord has the first three; say so.

Say the rent for the rest of the lease, through the end date.

Also: a suit cuts both ways, since the winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). The deposit may go toward the loss, since security deposits cover "monetary damage to the landlord caused by the tenant’s breach of lease prior to the expiration thereof." (83.43(14)), but only by the steps in 83.49(3); a lease clause that simply takes it is an early termination fee (above). After the move, deposit_not_returned covers those steps. Court steps and amounts are outside this tool.

A tenant who just stops coming may be treated as having abandoned the home: "In the absence of actual knowledge of abandonment, it shall be presumed that the tenant has abandoned the dwelling unit if he or she is absent from the premises for a period of time equal to one-half the time for periodic rental payments." (83.59(3)(c)), unless the rent is current or they told the landlord in writing of an intended absence (83.59(3)(c)). The landlord may remove what they leave behind after "surrender, abandonment" (83.67(5)); read the lease for a clause on it. A landlord need not pay deposit interest to a tenant who wrongfully ended the tenancy early (83.49(9)).

## Whichever way they leave: the 7 days' notice

Any tenant moving out before the end date, and any tenant with no set end date. It keeps the landlord's duty to send a notice about the deposit. Say in the same breath that it does not end the lease or stop the rent.

- Options 1 and 3 have their own written notice. The stored text does not say whether this one applies too; one written notice by hand or certified mail, with the address, in time for both, meets both.
- Option 2 says "immediately vacate" (83.63(1)) and that the landlord shall follow 83.49(3). Whether a tenant leaving at once still needs these 7 days is not settled. One: the rule names "any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term" (83.49(5)). The other: 83.63 sets its own terms.
- The rule: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)), the tenant "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
- The last day: count_days(planned_move_out, -7), counted back from the move. The stored text does not say whether a certified letter counts from mailing or arrival; handing it over, or mailing it early, meets both.
- Handed over or certified mail, with an address: met. E-mail only under the signed addendum in 83.505(1). A portal message, a text, or regular mail is not one of the ways named.
- The lease has a clause on notice before leaving: read it. A different rule for leaving governs. Whether a clause on some other notice, like the notice before paying a fee, is one that "otherwise provided" (83.49(5)) is not settled; one notice in time for both, by hand or certified mail, with the address, meets both.
- If it is missed: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying a tenant may end a lease with a set end date just by giving notice when no way out fits, or that the 7 days' notice ends the lease or stops the rent.
- Stating one total owed, saying which choice the landlord will make, or counting the months left or the rent left.
- Saying the landlord must re-rent the home in every case. The duty is in 83.595(2) only.
- Applying a fee, a charge, or a loss of the deposit without the separate signed addendum and the other conditions, or treating what the lease calls a charge as deciding what it is.
- Leaving out what is still owed with a fee (83.595(4)(a)), or the prorated rent for a servicemember (83.682(4)).
- Missing a way out the facts point to.
- Counting the 7 days forward from the notice instead of back from the move.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.
